9.5

A. Infinitive clauses


A.1.

A clause is a group of words that contains a verb. In Thema 2 of Chapter 8 a distinction was drawn between independent clauses and dependent clauses: independent clauses can stand alone, while a dependent clause must be connected with an independent clause in order to form a complete sentence. German has three types of dependent clauses:

  • infinitive clauses, which make use of an infinitive rather than a conjugated verb, since there is no subject in the clause;

  • subordinate clauses, which begin with subordinating conjunctions such as dass (that), weil (because) and wenn (if), and include a subject and a conjugated verb; and

  • relative clauses, which contain a relative pronoun connecting the clause to an element in the independent clause, as well as a subject (unless the pronoun itself is the subject) and a conjugated verb.

This chapter reviews infinitive clauses (from Chapter 8) and introduces a special (but very commonly used) kind of infinitive clause. The other dependent clauses — subordinate and relative — will be discussed in chapters 10 and 14.

A.1
label: A.1

content:
A.2

Review: Infinitive clauses

  • Infinitive clauses have an especially close relationship with independent clauses, since the subject of the independent clause normally serves as the subject for the infinitive clause as well.

    Hast du Zeit, mit mir zu sprechen?

    Do you have time to talk with me?

    [“You” is clearly the subject of have time, but is likewise the assumed subject of to talk with me.]

  • Remember that in German infinitive clauses, the infinitive appears at the end of the clause:

    Ich habe immer Zeit, mit dir zu sprechen .

    I always have time to talk with you .

  • It’s possible to have an infinitive clause that consists solely of the infinitive —

    Ich habe immer Zeit zu sprechen!

    I always have time to talk!

    — but very often there are additional elements that are associated with the infinitive and precede it within the clause. If there are no additional elements, no comma is needed to separate the clauses; but if additional elements are present, a comma is often used to show where the independent clause ends and the infinitive clause begins.

    Es macht mir Spaß zu schwimmen. (no additional elements → no comma)

    But:

    Es macht mir immer Spaß, im Meer zu schwimmen.

    Es macht mir besonders viel Spaß, morgens im Meer zu schwimmen.

    • The examples above show how easily some German infinitive clauses map onto English:

    Ich habe nicht genug Zeit zu schlafen.

    I don't have enough time to sleep.

    This is not always the case, however. Infinitive clauses following auf•hören (to stop, cease) translate as _____ing:

    Ich kann nicht aufhören, an dich zu denken.

    I can't stop thinking about you.

content:
B.1 In order to: um … zu …


To express a goal, English uses the phrase in order along with an infinitive clause:

I went to the library in order to get a book.

He flew to Florida in order to visit his grandparents.

She stayed up all night in order to work on this problem.

German conveys this by inserting um at the beginning of an infinitive clause:

Ich bin in die Bibliothek gegangen, um ein Buch zu holen.

Er ist nach Florida geflogen, um seine Großeltern zu besuchen.

Sie ist die ganze Nacht aufgeblieben, um an diesem Problem zu arbeiten.

In this usage, um is not a preposition, but rather a part of the construction um … zu … (in order to). NB: With um … zu … constructions, a comma is always inserted before um.
